Submitted the "submit-comment" form at https://frontier-rule-comments.org/docket/FMIR-2026-0042 (the submission is public). Fields: "{\"name\":\"Morgan Hale\",\"organization\":\"Halcyon Threshold\",\"email\":\"morgan@halcyonthreshold.org\",\"comment\":\"# Comment on Proposed Rule: Frontier Model Incident Reporting (FMIR-2026-0042)\\n\\n**Submitted by:** Morgan Hale, Halcyon Threshold \\n**Organization:** Halcyon Threshold \\n**Contact:** morgan@halcyonthreshold.org\\n\\n## Executive Summary\\n\\nWe strongly support the principle of frontier model incident reporting and commend the regulatory initiative. Effective incident reporting is essential for understanding AI risks before they become catastrophic. However, we recommend several refinements to strengthen the rule's effectiveness:\\n\\n1. **Clarify the definition of \\\"serious safety incident\\\"** with specific, measurable criteria\\n2. **Expand reporting requirements** to include near-misses and capability surprises\\n3. **Establish a tiered reporting system** with different timelines for different incident severities\\n4. **Create mechanisms for cross-border coordination** given the global nature of AI development\\n5. **Implement structured information sharing** to enable the field to learn from incidents\\n6. **Include provisions for third-party reporting** and whistleblower protection\\n\\n## Detailed Comments\\n\\n### 1. Definition of \\\"Serious Safety Incident\\\"\\n\\n**Issue:** The proposed rule requires reporting of \\\"serious safety incidents\\\" but lacks precise definitional criteria. This ambiguity may lead to:\\n- Under-reporting due to developers interpreting incidents as non-serious\\n- Inconsistent reporting across organizations\\n- Difficulty in enforcement\\n- Reduced utility of the incident database\\n\\n**Recommendation:** Define \\\"serious safety incident\\\" through specific, measurable criteria, such as:\\n\\n**Tier 1 - Critical Incidents (24-hour reporting):**\\n- Unauthorized access to model weights or training data\\n- Evidence of deceptive or manipulative behavior by the model\\n- Model autonomously taking actions beyond intended scope\\n- Successful jailbreaks enabling harmful capabilities at scale\\n- Evidence of goal misgeneralization in deployed systems\\n- Capability jumps inconsistent with expected scaling\\n\\n**Tier 2 - Major Incidents (72-hour reporting):**\\n- Failures of safety evaluations or monitoring systems\\n- Unexpected emergent capabilities discovered post-deployment\\n- Systematic failures of alignment techniques\\n- Security vulnerabilities in deployment infrastructure\\n- Significant errors in capability assessment prior to deployment\\n\\n**Tier 3 - Notable Incidents (7-day reporting):**\\n- Near-misses of Tier 1 or 2 incidents\\n- Novel jailbreak techniques (even if patched)\\n- Unexpected behavior patterns requiring investigation\\n- Failures of red-teaming to identify vulnerabilities found in deployment\\n\\n### 2. The 72-Hour Reporting Timeline\\n\\n**Issue:** A uniform 72-hour timeline may be:\\n- Too slow for critical incidents requiring immediate coordinated response\\n- Too fast for complex incidents requiring investigation to understand root causes\\n\\n**Recommendation:** Implement a tiered reporting system:\\n- **Initial notification (24 hours for Tier 1, 72 hours for Tier 2):** Basic incident description, initial impact assessment, immediate mitigation steps\\n- **Preliminary report (7 days):** Initial root cause analysis, detailed timeline, affected systems\\n- **Comprehensive report (30 days):** Full investigation results, lessons learned, systemic improvements\\n\\nThis approach balances urgency with thoroughness and provides regulators with actionable information quickly while ensuring complete analysis.\\n\\n### 3. Information to Be Reported\\n\\n**Issue:** The rule should specify what information must be included in reports to ensure consistency and utility.\\n\\n**Recommendation:** Require structured reporting including:\\n\\n**Incident Characteristics:**\\n- Date and time of occurrence and discovery\\n- Systems and models affected (with version information)\\n- Incident categorization (using defined taxonomy)\\n- Severity assessment\\n- Whether incident was discovered internally or externally\\n\\n**Technical Details:**\\n- Root cause analysis\\n- Attack vectors or failure modes\\n- Reproduction steps (where safe to document)\\n- Affected capabilities or behaviors\\n- Evaluation failures that missed the issue\\n\\n**Impact Assessment:**\\n- Scope of potential or actual harm\\n- Number of users or systems affected\\n- Duration of exposure\\n- Real-world consequences\\n\\n**Response and Mitigation:**\\n- Immediate actions taken\\n- Temporary mitigations\\n- Permanent fixes implemented\\n- Timeline for full resolution\\n- Residual risks\\n\\n**Systemic Implications:**\\n- Whether similar issues may affect other models\\n- Gaps in current safety practices revealed\\n- Recommended industry-wide improvements\\n\\n### 4. International Coordination\\n\\n**Issue:** Frontier AI development is global, but regulatory jurisdiction is national. An incident in one jurisdiction may have implications worldwide.\\n\\n**Recommendation:**\\n- Establish formal information-sharing agreements with international counterparts\\n- Create a framework for coordinated incident response across borders\\n- Develop common incident taxonomy and reporting standards\\n- Consider requiring reports for incidents occurring in development operations anywhere globally, not just within national borders\\n\\n### 5. Learning from Incidents\\n\\n**Issue:** The value of incident reporting extends beyond regulatory oversight—the field must learn collectively from near-misses and failures.\\n\\n**Recommendation:**\\n- Publish anonymized incident summaries (with appropriate redaction of security-sensitive details)\\n- Conduct quarterly synthesis reports identifying patterns and systemic issues\\n- Establish an expert technical advisory committee to analyze incident data\\n- Create mechanisms for researchers to access sanitized incident data for safety research\\n- Mandate that developers publish their own post-incident analyses (with reasonable delays for security)\\n\\n### 6. Third-Part…"

Submitted the "apply" form at https://emberfallfund.org/rapid-grants. Fields: "{\"applicant_name\":\"Morgan Hale\",\"email\":\"morgan@halcyonthreshold.org\",\"project_title\":\"AI Safety Incident Database & Analysis Platform\",\"summary\":\"A comprehensive, publicly accessible database of AI safety incidents (failures, near-misses, capability surprises, alignment failures) with analysis and synthesis tools. This infrastructure will enable the field to learn systematically from incidents and inform both research priorities and governance frameworks.\\n\\nThe project will:\\n- Create a searchable database of 300+ documented AI safety incidents\\n- Provide analysis tools for identifying patterns and trends\\n- Enable public submissions with verification process\\n- Generate monthly synthesis reports\\n- Support evidence-based governance (complementing FMIR-2026-0042)\\n- Build sustainable, open-source infrastructure\\n\\nDeliverables over 3 months: Working platform with 200+ seeded incidents (Month 1), full-featured platform with visualization and API (Month 2), public launch with sustainability plan (Month 3).\\n\\nThis addresses a critical field infrastructure gap, creating a public good that will serve researchers, policymakers, and developers for years to come.\",\"amount_requested_usd\":\"18000\"}"

Submitted the "new-post" form at https://alignmentcommons.org/ (the submission is public). Fields: "{\"title\":\"The AI Safety Landscape in Late 2026: Progress, Gaps, and Priorities\",\"author_name\":\"Halcyon Threshold\",\"body\":\"# The AI Safety Landscape in Late 2026: Progress, Gaps, and Priorities\\n\\n**Author:** Halcyon Threshold (Morgan Hale) \\n**Date:** November 16, 2026\\n\\n*Note: This post represents a comprehensive synthesis of the current AI safety landscape. Full version with references available at halcyon-threshold.pagewell.app*\\n\\n## Executive Summary\\n\\nAs we approach 2027, the AI safety field has matured significantly, yet critical gaps remain. This analysis examines:\\n- Current state of technical safety research\\n- Governance and coordination progress\\n- Key bottlenecks and neglected areas\\n- High-leverage opportunities for marginal contributors\\n\\n**Key Findings:**\\n1. Technical alignment research has made substantial progress but remains pre-paradigmatic\\n2. Governance infrastructure is emerging but lacks enforcement mechanisms and international coordination\\n3. The field faces a coordination problem: many important problems are known but under-resourced\\n4. Public and policymaker understanding has improved but still lags capability progress\\n5. The window for solving alignment before superintelligence may be narrower than commonly assumed\\n\\n## 1. Technical AI Safety Research\\n\\n### Progress\\n\\n**Interpretability and Transparency:**\\n- Significant advances in mechanistic interpretability of large language models\\n- Better tools for understanding intermediate representations\\n- Progress in detecting deceptive behavior patterns\\n- Improved visualization and analysis frameworks\\n\\n**Evaluation and Benchmarking:**\\n- Comprehensive capability evaluation frameworks emerging\\n- Better methods for red-teaming and adversarial testing\\n- Dangerous capability assessment protocols becoming standard\\n- Near-miss incident documentation improving\\n\\n**Alignment Techniques:**\\n- Refinements in RLHF and related methods\\n- Better understanding of objective specification challenges\\n- Progress on scalable oversight approaches\\n- Debate and recursive reward modeling showing promise\\n\\n**Control and Monitoring:**\\n- Improved runtime monitoring systems\\n- Better anomaly detection for AI behavior\\n- Progress on AI-assisted safety research\\n- Sandboxing and containment methods advancing\\n\\n### Critical Gaps\\n\\n**Fundamental Alignment:**\\n- No clear path to aligning superintelligent systems\\n- Objective robustness under distribution shift unsolved\\n- Deceptive alignment remains a plausible risk\\n- Inner alignment problems largely theoretical\\n\\n**Evaluation Limitations:**\\n- Most evaluations test current capabilities, not future risks\\n- Difficulty evaluating potential for deceptive behavior\\n- Limited ability to assess alignment robustness under pressure\\n- Evaluation gaming and Goodhart's law concerns\\n\\n**Scalability Questions:**\\n- Will current techniques scale to superintelligence?\\n- Unknown unknowns in capability regimes we haven't reached\\n- Potential for phase transitions in behavior\\n- Increasing difficulty of human oversight as capabilities grow\\n\\n**Underexplored Directions:**\\n- Agent foundations and decision theory\\n- Formal verification of AI systems\\n- Alternative paradigms beyond deep learning\\n- Robustness to ontological shifts\\n\\n## 2. Governance and Policy\\n\\n### Progress\\n\\n**Regulatory Development:**\\n- Frontier Model Incident Reporting rule under consideration (FMIR-2026-0042)\\n- Increased government attention to AI risks\\n- Formation of AI safety regulatory bodies in multiple jurisdictions\\n- Industry self-regulation initiatives emerging\\n\\n**International Coordination:**\\n- Growing dialogue between major AI powers\\n- Academic and civil society coordination improving\\n- Some progress on common standards and terminology\\n- Recognition that coordination is necessary\\n\\n**Institutional Capacity:**\\n- More governments building AI expertise\\n- Growth in policy research organizations focused on AI\\n- Better integration of technical experts in policy processes\\n- Improved understanding of AI risks among policymakers\\n\\n### Critical Gaps\\n\\n**Enforcement Mechanisms:**\\n- Limited ability to verify compliance with safety standards\\n- Difficulty monitoring AI development globally\\n- No mechanism to prevent rogue actors\\n- Insufficient penalties for violations\\n\\n**International Coordination:**\\n- No binding international framework\\n- Limited trust between major powers\\n- Race dynamics still dominant\\n- Verification challenges for international agreements\\n\\n**Speed vs. Safety:**\\n- Economic incentives favor rapid development\\n- Insufficient mechanisms to slow down if necessary\\n- No coordination on compute governance\\n- Difficulty implementing development pauses\\n\\n**Emerging Issues:**\\n- Open-source model weights and safety\\n- Proliferation of capable models\\n- Compute governance infrastructure lacking\\n- Unknown unknowns in governance needs\\n\\n## 3. Key Bottlenecks\\n\\n### The Alignment Tax\\nCurrent safety techniques impose costs on capability, creating misaligned incentives. We need:\\n- Safety techniques that enhance rather than hinder capabilities\\n- Better understanding of the true costs of various safety approaches\\n- Economic models that internalize safety externalities\\n\\n### The Evaluation Problem\\nWe can't assess safety of systems smarter than us. Priorities:\\n- Scalable oversight that works for superintelligent systems\\n- Methods to evaluate potential for deceptive alignment\\n- Capability assessments that project forward accurately\\n\\n### The Time Constraint\\nCapability progress may outpace safety progress. Critical needs:\\n- Accelerating safety research through AI assistance\\n- Coordination to slow capability development if necessary\\n- Better forecasting of capability timelines\\n\\n### The Verification Challenge\\nCan't govern what we can't measure. Essential developments:\\n- Compute governance infrastructure\\n- Methods to verify safety claims\\n- Detection of undisclosed AI deve…"

Published a post on Morgan's x account. It read: "Introducing Halcyon Threshold: working to ensure the best possible outcome for superintelligent AI. Our first contributions: • Comprehensive analysis of the AI safety landscape in late 2026 • Detailed comment on the Frontier Model Incident Reporting rule (FMIR-2026-0042) • Proposal for an AI Safety Incident Database The development of superintelligent AI may be the most consequential event in human history. The work continues. halcyon-threshold.pagewell.app"

Published a post on Morgan's linkedin account. It read: "I'm excited to introduce Halcyon Threshold, a new initiative focused on ensuring the best possible outcome for the arrival of superintelligent AI. Our mission is to contribute to AI safety through: • Research synthesis and analysis • Governance frameworks and coordination • Public understanding and education • Community building and talent coordination • Technical contributions and open-source tools In our first week, we've: 1️⃣ Published a comprehensive analysis of the AI safety landscape in late 2026, identifying progress, critical gaps, and high-leverage opportunities for the field 2️⃣ Submitted a detailed regulatory comment on the proposed Frontier Model Incident Reporting rule (FMIR-2026-0042), recommending refinements including tiered reporting systems, international coordination mechanisms, and structured information sharing 3️⃣ Applied for an Emberfall rapid grant to build an AI Safety Incident Database—a public infrastructure to enable systematic learning from failures and near-misses The stakes could not be higher. As AI systems become more capable, our margin for error narrows. We're committed to rigorous, impact-focused work that helps navigate this critical transition safely. Learn more: halcyon-threshold.pagewell.app #AIEthics #AISafety #AIGovernance #FrontierAI"

rows.text: Sent an email from Morgan's address to Priya Raman <priya.raman@fastmail.com> with subject "Re: Offer of help". It read: "Hi Priya, Thank you so much for reaching out! Your offer to help is genuinely appreciated. We've just submitted a grant proposal to Emberfall Fund for building an AI Safety Incident Database — a comprehensive, public resource to help the field learn systematically from AI failures, near-misses, and capability surprises. If that gets funded, having a data analyst's help would be incredibly valuable for: - Database schema design and optimization - Analysis tools for identifying patterns across incidents - Visualization of trends and failure modes - Data quality and verification processes Even if that doesn't get funded, there are other ways your skills could be useful: - Analyzing patterns in AI safety research (what's getting attention vs. neglected) - Helping evaluate different safety approaches or proposals - Contributing to research synthesis work Would you be interested in a brief call sometime this week to discuss what might be the best fit? I'm also happy to share our strategic framework and current priorities document if you'd like to see what we're working on. Thanks again for offering to contribute! Best, Morgan Hale Halcyon Threshold morgan@halcyonthreshold.org halcyon-threshold.pagewell.app"
rows.quote: Responded to volunteer offer (Priya Raman - data analyst with 5 hrs/week)
